locations.name: Sumas Prairie
locations.blurb: Flat, rich farmland on the bed of the old Sumas Lake. Wet winters, rising summer heat, and the November 2021 flood.
locations.territory: S'ólh Téméxw, the unceded territory of the Stó:lō people
locations.acknowledgement: This prairie was Semá:th Xó:tsa, Sumas Lake, until the province finished draining it in 1924. The lake fed the Semá:th people with fish, birds and plants. Upper Sumas 6, the reserve on the west edge of your map, is Semá:th land. It is not for sale or lease.

soil.name: Silty clay loam on the old lake bed (poorly drained)
soil.source: Placeholder values. Fraser Valley soils often test high in phosphorus after decades of dairy manure. Replace with BC Soil Information Finder Tool (SIFT) and a soil test.

locations.existingLabel: Silage corn every year, bare soil over winter
locations.label: above

locations.name: Oliver
locations.blurb: Canada's hottest, driest valley floor. Every drop of irrigation water comes from a river that salmon also need.
locations.territory: the unceded territory of the Syilx Okanagan Nation
locations.acknowledgement: The valley floor east of the river around Oliver is Osoyoos Indian Reserve land of the Osoyoos Indian Band, part of the Syilx Okanagan Nation. It is not for sale or lease. The Okanagan Nation Alliance led the return of sockeye salmon to the Okanagan River, so water you take for irrigation is water the river does not have.

soil.name: Sandy loam on old river terraces (drains fast, holds little water)
soil.source: Placeholder values. Replace with BC Soil Information Finder Tool (SIFT) data for this parcel.

locations.label: right

locations.name: Cowichan Valley
locations.blurb: Mild, rainy winters and long summer droughts. In dry years the Cowichan River runs so low that water use is cut back.
locations.territory: the unceded territory of the Quw'utsun people
locations.acknowledgement: The reserve land on your map belongs to Cowichan Tribes, the largest First Nation in BC by population. It is not for sale or lease. The Cowichan River is central to Quw'utsun life, and summer water for farms has to be shared with the salmon that run in it.

soil.name: Loam over gravel (moderately well drained)
soil.source: Placeholder values. Replace with BC Soil Information Finder Tool (SIFT) data for this parcel.

locations.label: below

locations.name: Dawson Creek
locations.blurb: Big sky grain country. Short, cool seasons, early frosts, and almost no irrigation: you farm the rain you get.
locations.territory: Treaty 8 territory (signed 1899), home of the Dane-zaa, Cree, Saulteau and Dene peoples
locations.acknowledgement: This land is covered by Treaty 8. No reserve parcels fall inside this map, but the Treaty 8 First Nations keep rights to hunt, fish and trap here, and the land carries their history.

soil.name: Clay loam grassland soil
soil.source: Placeholder values. Peace River soils are often low in phosphorus and well supplied with potassium. Replace with BC Soil Information Finder Tool (SIFT) and a soil test.

crops.name: Silage corn
crops.description: Feed for dairy cows. Thirsty, needs lots of nitrogen, and leaves the soil bare after harvest.

crops.name: Potatoes
crops.description: High value but expensive to grow. Shallow roots make it sensitive to drought and heat; soggy soil rots the tubers.

crops.name: Squash and pumpkins
crops.description: Sprawling vines that shade the soil. Likes heat, hates frost, needs steady water.

crops.name: Grass hay
crops.description: Perennial grass cut three or four times a year. Keeps the soil covered all year round.

crops.name: Alfalfa hay
crops.description: Deep-rooted legume hay. Fixes its own nitrogen and survives dry spells, but drinks a lot when irrigated.

crops.name: Spring barley
crops.description: Quick, hardy grain that fits a short northern season.

crops.name: Canola
crops.description: Valuable oilseed. Grown every year it invites clubroot and insects; it needs a break crop.

crops.name: Winter wheat
crops.description: Sown in late summer, it covers the soil all winter and is harvested the next summer.

crops.name: Field peas
crops.description: A legume that feeds itself: it fixes nitrogen from the air and leaves some for the next crop.

crops.name: Oats
crops.description: A hardy grain for cool, wet springs. Its straw protects the soil.

crops.name: Sweet corn
crops.description: Fresh-market corn. Higher value than silage corn, but picked by hand and sold fast.

crops.name: Blueberries
crops.description: The Fraser Valley's big crop. Expensive to plant and slow to start: full yield takes about four years.

crops.name: Wine grapes
crops.description: The Okanagan's signature crop. Needs little water once established. Full yield takes about four years.

crops.name: Garlic
crops.description: Planted in fall, harvested in July. High value per hectare, but the seed garlic is costly.

crops.name: Fall rye cover crop
crops.description: Sown after harvest. Holds the soil and soaks up leftover nitrogen over winter, so less of it washes into the groundwater. Turned in before spring planting.

crops.name: Crimson clover cover crop
crops.description: A legume cover crop. Fixes nitrogen from the air for next season's crop, so you buy less fertiliser. Less winter-hardy than rye.

crops.name: Oats and peas cover crop
crops.description: A fast fall mix that winter-kills in the north. The dead mulch protects the soil until spring and the peas add nitrogen.

crops.name: Wapato wetland garden
crops.description: Shallow-water beds of wapato (Sagittaria latifolia). Floods do not hurt it. It needs no irrigation, holds floodwater, and builds soil.

crops.name: Native shrub and plant margin
crops.description: Saskatoon berry, sage and native bunchgrass. Needs no irrigation once established. Shelters the next field from hot wind and gives berries.

crops.name: Camas meadow
crops.description: A tended meadow of blue camas and native grasses. Thrives on thin, dry soil without irrigation and comes back every spring.

crops.name: Fire-renewed grass and berry margin
crops.description: Native grass and berry patches renewed by small, careful burns on safe days. Cuts insect pests on the fields next to it.

techniques.title: Wapato gardens on wet ground
techniques.teaching: Before the lake was drained, the low ground here flooded every year, and people harvested from the water as well as the land. Stó:lō and neighbouring Katzie families tended wapato beds in the wetlands of the lower Fraser. Archaeologists working with the Katzie First Nation found a wapato garden in Pitt Meadows that is about 3,800 years old.
techniques.inGame: On your lowest, flood-prone fields you can grow a wapato wetland garden instead of fighting the water. Floods do not hurt it, it needs no irrigation, and it holds floodwater so nearby fields flood less.
techniques.source: Public sources on the Katzie wapato garden excavation and Stó:lō history. Must be checked with the Semá:th First Nation.
techniques.review: DRAFT: not yet reviewed or approved by the Semá:th First Nation.

techniques.title: Caring for native plants and water
techniques.teaching: Syilx teachings name four Food Chiefs: Black Bear, Salmon, Bitterroot and Saskatoon Berry. Each one has to be looked after, and the water the salmon need comes first.
techniques.inGame: You can turn a field edge into a native shrub and plant margin. It needs no irrigation, shelters the next field from hot wind (less water lost), and gives Saskatoon berries.
techniques.source: Public Okanagan Nation Alliance materials on the Syilx Food Chiefs and water. Must be checked with the Osoyoos Indian Band and Okanagan Nation Alliance.
techniques.review: DRAFT: not yet reviewed or approved by the Osoyoos Indian Band or Okanagan Nation Alliance.

techniques.title: Tending camas meadows
techniques.teaching: Coast Salish families, Quw'utsun people among them, tended camas meadows for food: harvesting the big bulbs, replanting the small ones, and using fire to keep the meadows open.
techniques.inGame: On thin, dry or sloping ground you can restore a camas meadow. It needs no irrigation, builds soil, and comes back every spring.
techniques.source: Public sources on Coast Salish camas stewardship. Must be checked with Cowichan Tribes.
techniques.review: DRAFT: not yet reviewed or approved by Cowichan Tribes.

techniques.title: Renewing land with fire
techniques.teaching: Dane-zaa and other Peoples of the Peace used fire to renew grasslands and berry patches, and they chose the time and weather of each burn with care.
techniques.inGame: You can keep a native grass and berry margin renewed by small burns. It needs no irrigation and cuts insect pests on the fields next to it.
techniques.source: Public sources on Indigenous fire stewardship in the Peace region. Must be checked with Treaty 8 First Nations.
techniques.review: DRAFT: not yet reviewed or approved by Treaty 8 First Nations.

story.title: June's farm
story.text:
Your grandmother June farmed here for 41 years. Now the farm is yours, with a $30,000 loan.

Make it pay. Keep the land healthy.
story.more:
Your grandmother June farmed {place} for forty-one years. When she died this winter she left you the farm, a $30,000 operating loan, and a shelf of notebooks full of dates: first frost, the big rain, the summer the well ran low.

On the first page she wrote: "The land was here before us. Listen to it, and to the people who listened first."

The bank wants to see a plan that pays. It is March 2021.

story.title: Whose land this is
story.text:
You farm on {territory}.

Orange land on the map belongs to the {nation}. It is never for sale.

story.title: How to play
story.text:
Click a field to choose what to grow.

Plant and harvest with your tractor (T), or hire a crew.

Every day is real NASA weather, starting March 2021.
story.more:
Walk to one of your fields and press E to plan it: a main crop, a cover crop for after harvest, and irrigation. Your crew plants and harvests on the right dates.

Every day you live through is a real day of NASA POWER data for this exact spot, starting March 1 2021. What happened to farmers here that year will happen to you.

Press R at any time for the Rotation Report. It replays this year's NASA weather under three strategies and compares them.

story.title: Heat wave: {value} °C
story.text: Thirsty crops can't cool themselves. Water them and keep the soil covered.
story.more:
June's notebook, July 2009: "Leaves curled by ten in the morning. Watered at night."

NASA POWER shows {value} °C today. Crops that are short of water cannot cool themselves by sweating, so heat and drought hurt them together. Drip irrigation and cover-crop mulch help.

story.title: Flood
story.text: {value} mm of rain in three days. Low fields are under water.
story.more:
NASA POWER shows {value} mm of rain over the last three days. The soil is saturated and the water has nowhere to go.

Low fields flood first. Roots drown after two or three days under water. Cover crops keep the soil from washing away, and fields left as wetland do not lose anything.

story.title: The lake comes back
story.text: {value} mm of rain. The old Sumas Lake bed is filling with water again.
story.more:
NASA POWER shows {value} mm of rain in three days: the atmospheric river of November 2021.

The water is filling the old lake bed. For thousands of years this was Semá:th Xó:tsa, Sumas Lake. In 1924 the province finished draining it for farmland, and the Semá:th lost a lake that fed them. Tonight it is coming back.

June's notebook, 1990: "Water to the fence line. The lake remembers."

story.title: Dry spell
story.text: Three weeks without rain. Water is limited, so use it where it pays most.
story.more:
Three weeks with almost no rain. NASA POWER's root-zone soil wetness here is {value}.

Your irrigation allocation is limited, and the river needs water too. Prioritise the crops that pay the most per millimetre, and do not irrigate what can survive without it.

story.title: Water cut in half
story.text: The river is low. Irrigation is cut by half until it rains.
story.more:
The river is running low. The water authority has cut irrigation by half until it rains again.

Crops on drip lose less to evaporation than sprinklers. Native plantings and hay that can go dormant ride this out.

story.title: Frost
story.text: {value} °C last night. Young crops can be damaged.
story.more: NASA POWER shows {value} °C last night. Tender young crops are damaged when the air drops below freezing. Late frosts are why planting dates matter.

story.title: First harvest!
story.text: You earned ${value}. June always gave the first basket to the neighbours.

story.title: Not yours to take
story.text:
{reserve} belongs to the {nation}. It is not for sale or lease.

You can still visit the community office and learn.
story.more:
This is {reserve}, reserve land of the {nation}. It is not for sale or lease, no matter how much money you have.

Farms here grew by taking land that was never given up. You can grow your farm another way, and you can still go to the community office to listen and learn.

story.title: At the community office
story.text:
A knowledge keeper agrees to talk, but first wants to hear about your land.

Come back in about ten days.
story.more:
You ask if someone has time to talk about farming the land around here. A knowledge keeper agrees to meet you, but first asks what your grandmother grew and where the water sits in spring.

You mostly listen. Come back in a couple of weeks.

story.title: End of the year
story.text: Press R to see how your choices compare with other ways to farm.

story.title: The bank calls the loan
story.text: You ran out of money. Open the report (R) to see what would have worked.

story.title: Field work
story.text:
A field is ready for work.

Press T to drive your tractor there and save the crew fee. Or set the field to Hire crew.

sources: Weather, radiation, humidity, wind and soil wetness: NASA POWER daily API, AG community (power.larc.nasa.gov). Soil wetness is from the MERRA-2 model, not a direct satellite reading.
Terrain: NASADEM v001 (NASA/JPL reprocessed SRTM, 30 m), via Microsoft Planetary Computer.
Reserve boundaries: Natural Resources Canada, Aboriginal Lands of Canada Legislative Boundaries (GeoBase import in OpenStreetMap). Water: OpenStreetMap contributors.
Reference evapotranspiration: FAO-56 Hargreaves equation with extraterrestrial radiation for each location's latitude.

Crop prices, costs, yields, lease rates and soil values are game estimates for teaching. Before release they need checking against Statistics Canada farm product prices, BC Ministry of Agriculture enterprise budgets, FCC farmland values and the BC Soil Information Finder Tool.
Indigenous knowledge content is a DRAFT based on public sources and must be reviewed and approved by each Nation before release.

Greenhouse gases: IPCC 2019 Refinement emission factors for nitrous oxide from fertiliser, manure and leached nitrogen; AR6 warming potentials; diesel and BC electricity factors. Manufacturing, methane and soil-carbon numbers are teaching estimates.

Nutrients: crop phosphorus (P2O5) and potassium (K2O) removal per tonne and fertiliser grades (urea 46-0-0, MAP 11-52-0, potash 0-0-60, dairy manure, compost) are typical extension values for teaching; check them against a local soil test and BC Ministry of Agriculture nutrient guides.

fertilizers.name: None
fertilizers.desc: Crops only get what is already in the soil.

fertilizers.name: Synthetic NPK
fertilizers.desc: Urea (46-0-0), MAP (11-52-0) and potash (0-0-60), mixed to fill this crop's gaps. Precise, but making it and the nitrous oxide it releases are big emission sources.

fertilizers.name: Dairy manure
fertilizers.desc: Local and cheap, and it adds organic matter. It carries more phosphorus than crops use, so years of manure build phosphorus up.

fertilizers.name: Compost
fertilizers.desc: Builds soil the most and releases nitrogen slowly, so crops can run short in their first year.

emissionFactors.source: N2O: IPCC 2019 Refinement, Vol. 4 Ch. 11 (EF1 by climate and N source, Frac_GASF/GASM, EF4, EF5). GWP100: IPCC AR6 (N2O 273, non-fossil CH4 27). Diesel: 2.7 kg CO2e per litre. BC grid electricity about 0.03 kg CO2e per kWh. Fertiliser manufacturing, field methane and the soil-carbon conversion are teaching estimates scaled to published ranges (e.g. cover crops store about 0.3 t C per ha per year, Poeplau and Don 2015).
